title: America Is Burning Through Its Emergency Oil Reserves at Record Speed. Half the Crude Is Being Shipped Overseas.
excerpt: The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has dropped to 365 million barrels after back-to-back record weekly drawdowns. By the time the current release programme ends, reserves will hit their lowest level since the 1980s. Here is what NRI investors should understand.
body:
The United States has released nearly 50 million barrels of crude oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively shut down in late February. The SPR now holds 365 million barrels — roughly half its authorised capacity of 714 million, and the lowest level since April 2024.

The numbers from the last two weeks are particularly striking. The week ending May 15 saw the largest single-week drawdown in the SPR's history: 9.92 million barrels. The following week saw another 9.1 million barrels drained. For context, the previous all-time weekly record was 7.41 million barrels, set during the Ukraine crisis in October 2022.

What makes this drawdown different from any in SPR history is that approximately half the crude being released is not staying in the United States. It is being exported.

## America as the World's Oil Supplier of Last Resort

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly 20 per cent of the world's oil supply passes — has forced countries in Europe and Asia to scramble for alternative sources. The US has stepped into that gap more aggressively than at any point since the SPR was created in 1975.

US crude exports briefly hit a record 6.4 million barrels per day, according to Kpler, the energy intelligence firm. An armada of tankers has been pulling American crude toward refineries in Europe and Asia, where countries that previously relied on Middle Eastern oil have been forced to find alternatives.

The US government has committed to releasing 172 million barrels from the SPR on a loan basis as part of an international response to the crisis. So far, about 50 million barrels of that commitment have been fulfilled.

"The US is basically the supplier of last resort. The rest of the world needs that crude," said Matt Smith, an oil analyst at Kpler.

## The Math Is Getting Tight

By the time the full 172-million-barrel release programme is complete, the SPR will hold roughly 300 million barrels — the lowest level since the 1980s. Sarah Emerson, president of ESAI Energy, notes that 300 million barrels is "still a hefty amount of oil," but the margin of safety is narrowing rapidly.

The practical concern is not that America will run out of oil. It is that the emergency buffer — the thing that is supposed to be there for the next crisis — is being used up to manage this one. Kevin Liu, an oil and gas analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, compared the releases to painkillers: "It helps relieve the immediate pressure, but it does not solve the underlying supply tension."

Meanwhile, commercial crude inventories are tightening independently. Total US crude stocks fell 7.88 million barrels in the most recent weekly report, the fourth consecutive weekly draw. Gasoline inventories are near six-month lows. Cushing, Oklahoma — the key pricing hub for US oil — is watching storage levels fall as refinery runs stay high.

## What Happens If the Strait Stays Closed?

The optimistic scenario is already partially priced in. A plan to extend the US-Iran ceasefire by 60 days and reopen the Strait of Hormuz was reportedly awaiting President Trump's approval as of last Friday. Brent crude fell to around $91 per barrel on that news, down roughly 20 per cent from its May peak.

But analysts are cautious about treating the deal as done. The ceasefire is better described as a pause than a settlement.

If the Strait remains closed through the summer, the outlook shifts dramatically. ESAI Energy's Emerson has warned that oil could reach $140 to $150 per barrel in a protracted-conflict scenario. The EIA's own models project Brent averaging $106 in May and June before falling to $89 by Q4 — but that forecast assumes the disruption is temporary.

The IEA's May report contained an even more striking data point: global oil demand is projected to contract by 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in 2026, falling to 104 million barrels per day. If confirmed, this would be the first global demand contraction in years, driven by high prices destroying consumption.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

For Indian Americans with exposure to energy, equities, and the Indian economy, the SPR drawdown matters in several interconnected ways.

**India's import bill.** India is the world's third-largest oil importer. Crude above $90 per barrel translates directly into a wider current account deficit, higher fuel prices, and inflationary pressure. The rupee has already lost more than 5 per cent this year, and overseas investors have pulled $24 billion from Indian debt and equities between March and May.

**The RBI's rate decision.** The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee meets June 3-5. A Reuters poll of 56 economists found that 44 expect the repo rate to be held at 5.25 per cent, but a growing minority — 11 out of 56 — now forecast a 25-basis-point hike. Capital Economics has a base case of the RBI raising rates to 6.00 per cent before year-end if the crisis persists. Elevated oil prices are the single biggest variable in that decision.

**US energy stocks.** Companies exposed to domestic oil production, refining, and export infrastructure have benefited from the crisis. But if the Strait reopens and crude drops back toward $70-80, many of those gains could reverse quickly. NRI investors holding energy-heavy portfolios should consider their exposure to a normalisation scenario.

**Gold as a hedge.** India just raised gold import duty to 15 per cent, crushing domestic demand. But gold has historically performed well during periods of geopolitical uncertainty and currency weakness. For NRI families planning weddings or remittances, the timing of gold purchases matters more than usual.

## The Bigger Picture

The SPR was designed to be America's insurance policy against exactly this kind of disruption. It has performed that function twice in four years — first during the Ukraine war, now during the Iran crisis. Each time, the policy response has been to draw down the reserve rather than address the underlying supply vulnerability.

The US has not meaningfully rebuilt its emergency stocks since the Biden-era drawdowns of 2022-23. The reserve went from 638 million barrels in January 2021 to 347 million by July 2023, recovered modestly, and is now falling again.

At some point, the painkiller stops working. For NRI investors, the question is not whether oil markets will stabilise — eventually, they will. The question is how much of America's emergency buffer will be left when the next crisis arrives, and what that means for a world that has come to depend on the US as its supplier of last resort.
